questions.stem: Annual rainfall in Tasmania's western mountains exceeds 3000 mm in places, while parts of the Midlands receive under 600 mm. What mainly causes this pattern?
options: Westerly winds rise over the western ranges and drop their rain, leaving a rain shadow in the east
Warm ocean currents along the east coast evaporate moisture away from the eastern half of the island
Higher temperatures in the west increase evaporation from the soil, which then falls back as local rain
The east lies closer to the equator, so it sits under dry subtropical high pressure for most of the year
questions.explanation: Moist westerly airstreams are forced up over the western mountains, cool and release much of their moisture. Air descending into the Midlands and east is drier, creating a rain shadow. The east is not meaningfully closer to the equator than the west.

questions.stem: A student maps vegetation across Tasmania from Strahan on the west coast to Ross in the Midlands. Which sequence is she most likely to record?
options: Dry sclerophyll and grassland in the west, wet sclerophyll in between, then rainforest and buttongrass across the dry Midlands
Grassland in the west, rainforest across the central highlands, then wet sclerophyll forest in the Midlands
Alpine heath in the west, buttongrass in between, then rainforest and mixed forest in the Midlands
Rainforest and buttongrass in the west, wet sclerophyll in between, then dry sclerophyll and grassland in the Midlands
questions.explanation: Vegetation follows the rainfall gradient. Rainforest, mixed forest and buttongrass moorland dominate the wet west, while dry sclerophyll forest and lowland grassland occupy the drier Midlands and east. Rainforest needs high, reliable rainfall, so it is absent from the dry Midlands.

questions.stem: On a hill near Hobart, dry sclerophyll forest grows on the north-facing slope and wet sclerophyll forest on the south-facing slope. What best explains the difference?
options: South-facing slopes have older soils because erosion is slower where frost forms through winter
North-facing slopes in the southern hemisphere get more direct sun, so they are warmer and drier
South-facing slopes in the southern hemisphere receive more direct sun, so plants there grow taller
North-facing slopes receive more rain because westerly winds strike them first on their way inland
questions.explanation: In the southern hemisphere the sun is to the north, so north-facing slopes receive more solar radiation, lose more soil moisture and carry drier, more fire-prone vegetation. South-facing slopes stay cooler and moister, favouring wet forest.

questions.stem: Two sites at the same altitude receive the same rainfall. Site X is a steep, north-facing ridge with shallow soil; site Y is a sheltered south-facing gully with deep soil. Which prediction is best supported?
options: Site X carries more fire-prone, open forest, and site Y is more likely to hold rainforest species
Site X is more likely to hold rainforest species, and site Y carries more fire-prone, open forest
Both sites carry the same forest type, because rainfall alone determines Tasmanian vegetation
Site X carries taller trees, because steep slopes drain water towards the roots of the canopy
questions.explanation: Equal rainfall does not mean equal moisture. The exposed ridge is sunnier, drier and has shallow soil, so it dries out and burns more often. The sheltered gully holds moisture and is protected from fire, so fire-sensitive rainforest species can persist there.

questions.stem: Dry sclerophyll forest in eastern Tasmania is best described as:
options: treeless sedgeland dominated by tussocks on waterlogged, peaty soils of the west
tall eucalypt forest over a dense understorey of rainforest trees, burnt only once every few centuries
open eucalypt forest with a shrubby or grassy understorey, adapted to frequent, low-intensity fire
closed forest of myrtle beech and sassafras with a mossy floor, rarely or never burnt
questions.explanation: Dry sclerophyll forest has an open eucalypt canopy with hard-leaved shrubs or grasses below, in lower-rainfall areas. It burns relatively often at low intensity. The closed myrtle and sassafras forest describes cool temperate rainforest.

questions.stem: After a low-intensity fire in dry sclerophyll forest, many eucalypts are green again within weeks. Which adaptation mainly allows this?
options: Shallow roots spread rapidly across the ash bed and send up new stems from the surface
Epicormic buds under thick bark sprout new shoots along the trunk and branches
Seeds stored in the soil for decades germinate only after rain has fallen on the ash
Leaves with thin cuticles absorb water quickly and regrow from the burnt leaf tips
questions.explanation: Many eucalypts have dormant epicormic buds protected by bark, which sprout after fire so the canopy recovers quickly. Seed germination produces new plants, not regrowth on existing trees, and takes much longer to rebuild the canopy.

questions.stem: Wet sclerophyll forest in Tasmania typically has:
options: a tall eucalypt canopy over a moist understorey of broad-leaved shrubs and tree ferns
a low eucalypt canopy over an understorey of tussock grasses and scattered wildflowers
no eucalypts at all, with a canopy formed entirely of myrtle beech and celery-top pine
a canopy of cushion plants and small conifers on exposed, frost-prone mountain tops
questions.explanation: Wet sclerophyll forest has tall eucalypts such as Eucalyptus regnans or E. obliqua over a dense, moist understorey with broad-leaved shrubs and tree ferns. A forest with no eucalypts and a myrtle canopy is rainforest.

questions.stem: Eucalyptus regnans in Tasmania's wet forests is killed by intense fire but regenerates densely afterwards. Why does it depend on fire to regenerate?
options: Its roots are protected underground, so fire removes competitors while every adult resprouts from the base
Its seedlings are poisonous to herbivores only after fire, so they escape grazing during the first season
Its seedlings need the bare, sunlit ash bed left after fire and cannot establish under a dense shady understorey
Its seeds need chemicals in smoke to soften the seed coat, and no other cue can ever trigger the seeds to germinate
questions.explanation: E. regnans is a fire-killed obligate seeder. Fire releases seed from capsules in the crown and clears the understorey, giving seedlings the light and bare mineral soil they need. Without fire, shade-tolerant rainforest plants fill the understorey and eucalypt seedlings fail.

questions.stem: Mixed forest in Tasmania is a mature eucalypt overstorey above a rainforest understorey. It develops mainly when:
options: a wet forest site goes a long time without fire, so rainforest trees grow up under the old eucalypts
a rainforest burns often, so eucalypts invade the canopy while the rainforest plants survive in the shade below
grazing removes the shrub layer, so rainforest trees and eucalypts can establish together
a dry forest site receives extra rainfall for a few years, so eucalypts grow taller than usual
questions.explanation: Mixed forest reflects a long fire-free interval: rainforest species establish beneath eucalypts that regenerated after the last fire. Frequent fire would remove the fire-sensitive rainforest understorey, not create it.

questions.stem: A wet forest stand near Geeveston has a 250-year-old Eucalyptus regnans canopy over myrtle beech and sassafras, but no young eucalypts. If no fire occurs for several more centuries, what is the most likely outcome?
options: The understorey thins out, and the stand turns into an open dry sclerophyll forest
The myrtle beech dies back from lack of fire, and buttongrass moorland replaces the stand
The eucalypts die of old age without replacement and the stand becomes cool temperate rainforest
Eucalypt seedlings eventually establish in the deep shade, and the canopy stays dominated by eucalypts
questions.explanation: Without fire, shade-tolerant rainforest species keep regenerating while the light-demanding eucalypts cannot, so the stand undergoes succession to rainforest as the old eucalypts die. Eucalypt seedlings fail under a dense, shady understorey.

questions.stem: Which tree is the most common canopy dominant in Tasmania's cool temperate rainforest?
options: Silver wattle (Acacia dealbata)
Silver banksia (Banksia marginata)
Myrtle beech (Nothofagus cunninghamii)
Swamp gum (Eucalyptus regnans)
questions.explanation: Myrtle beech is the characteristic dominant of Tasmanian cool temperate rainforest, often with sassafras, leatherwood and celery-top pine. Swamp gum is a eucalypt of wet sclerophyll forest, and wattles and banksias are not rainforest dominants.

questions.stem: Why is cool temperate rainforest largely restricted to western and north-western Tasmania and sheltered gullies elsewhere?
options: It needs nutrient-poor peat, which forms only where buttongrass has burnt many times
It needs high, reliable rainfall and long fire-free periods, which the wet west and sheltered sites provide
It needs fertile soil that is renewed by frequent fire, which happens most often in the wettest parts of the west
It needs very cold winters with heavy snow, which occur only at sea level on the west coast
questions.explanation: Rainforest needs plentiful rainfall spread through the year, and most of its species are killed by fire and recover slowly. The wet west and protected gullies burn rarely. Frequent fire favours eucalypts and buttongrass, not rainforest.

questions.stem: In 2016, fires burnt parts of Tasmania's rainforest and alpine vegetation that had not burnt for centuries. Why do ecologists regard such fires as a long-term loss rather than part of a normal fire cycle?
options: Many of these species lack fire adaptations and recover only over centuries, if at all, so repeated fire can eliminate them
These species depend on fire to release seed, so the fires simply restarted a natural cycle that normally takes a few decades
Fire in these areas adds nutrients that eucalypts cannot use, so the burnt sites stay bare for a few seasons
These species resprout vigorously after fire, so the fires mainly increase competition between neighbouring plants
questions.explanation: Rainforest and alpine conifers such as pencil pine evolved where fire was rare. After severe fire, few stems resprout and seedling regeneration is poor, so recovery may take centuries or fail. Unlike eucalypt forests, these communities have no fire-dependent regeneration cycle.

questions.stem: Fagus (Nothofagus gunnii), found in Tasmania's mountains, is notable because it is:
options: Australia's tallest flowering plant, reaching heights greater than any other native species
a fire-dependent eucalypt that releases its seed only after an intense crown fire
an introduced European beech that has invaded alpine heath and displaced native shrubs
Australia's only native winter-deciduous tree, turning gold and dropping its leaves in autumn
questions.explanation: Fagus is a native beech endemic to Tasmania and is Australia's only native cold-climate winter-deciduous tree. The tallest flowering plants in Australia are eucalypts such as E. regnans, not fagus.

questions.stem: Buttongrass moorland covers large areas of western Tasmania. It grows mainly on:
options: deep, well-drained basalt soils rich in nutrients
dry, sandy coastal soils that are often salty
fertile river flats renewed by regular flooding
wet, poorly drained, nutrient-poor organic soils
questions.explanation: Buttongrass (Gymnoschoenus sphaerocephalus) dominates wet, poorly drained, nutrient-poor organic soils in the west. Fertile, well-drained soils in the same rainfall zone tend to support forest instead.

questions.stem: Buttongrass burns readily and recovers quickly. How does frequent fire help keep moorland dominated by buttongrass?
options: Frequent fire depletes soil nutrients and removes plants that are less fire-tolerant than buttongrass
Frequent fire adds nutrients to the soil, and buttongrass is the only moorland plant able to take them up
Frequent fire raises the water table, drowning the roots of shrubs and trees nearby
Frequent fire kills the buttongrass seed bank, preventing any other sedges from establishing
questions.explanation: Repeated burning removes nutrients and favours fire-adapted buttongrass over less fire-tolerant shrubs and trees, maintaining moorland. Fire does release some nutrients in ash, but over repeated fires the net effect on these soils is depletion.

questions.stem: A ranger notices that a buttongrass moorland unburnt for 60 years now has scattered scrub, while a nearby moorland burnt every 10-15 years has none. A dry-season wildfire then burns down into the peat of the older site. What do these observations together show?
options: Buttongrass needs no fire at all, and scrub invades only after fire has removed the peat layer
Peat fires are harmless because buttongrass resprouts from seeds stored deep in the burnt organic soil
Long fire-free periods allow succession towards scrub, but a fire in very dry conditions can destroy the organic soil itself
Frequent fire allows succession towards scrub, while long fire-free periods protect the organic soil from damage
questions.explanation: Without fire, scrub and forest species gradually invade moorland. Long-unburnt moorland also builds up fuel, and a fire in drought can burn the organic soil, causing long-term damage that ordinary fires do not. This is why fire interval and timing both matter.

questions.stem: Lowland native grasslands of Tasmania, found mainly in the Midlands and east, are dominated by:
options: sedges such as buttongrass on peaty soil
cushion plants and low alpine heath shrubs
introduced pasture grasses such as ryegrass
tussock grasses such as kangaroo grass and poa
questions.explanation: These grasslands are dominated by native tussock grasses including kangaroo grass (Themeda triandra) and poa species. Buttongrass is a sedge of western moorlands, and cushion plants belong to alpine vegetation.

questions.stem: Lowland Native Grasslands of Tasmania are listed as critically endangered under national environment law. What is the main reason?
options: Most of the original grassland has been cleared or modified for agriculture, leaving small fragments
The grasslands lie in the wet west, where frequent flooding and waterlogging have drowned most of the remnants
The grasslands are being replaced by rainforest as the Midlands become steadily wetter
Kangaroo grass is a short-lived annual that cannot set seed in Tasmania's climate
questions.explanation: The flat, fertile Midlands were largely converted to cropping and improved pasture after European settlement, so the community survives mostly as small fragmented remnants. The Midlands are among the driest parts of the state, not the wettest.

questions.stem: Which set of conditions most shapes Tasmania's alpine vegetation on the Central Plateau and western mountains?
options: Salt spray, tidal flooding, shifting sand and strong onshore winds
Dense shade, deep leaf litter, high humidity and very low wind speeds
Low temperatures, frost, snow, strong winds and shallow or waterlogged soils
High temperatures, long droughts, frequent fire and deep, fertile soils
questions.explanation: Alpine plants face cold, frost, snow and wind with a short growing season, on thin rocky or boggy soils. This favours low cushion plants, bolster heath and small conifers. Salt spray and shifting sand describe coastal dunes.

questions.stem: Many alpine plants in Tasmania grow as low, tightly packed cushions. How does this growth form help them survive?
options: It raises the leaves above the snow so they can photosynthesise all winter
It lets the plant store fire-resistant seed in woody capsules for decades
It increases the leaf surface exposed to the wind so more water evaporates
It reduces exposure to wind and traps warmth and moisture close to the plant
questions.explanation: A dense, low cushion sits in the still air near the ground, reducing wind chill and water loss, and keeps warmth and moisture inside. Raising leaves into the wind would increase exposure, not reduce it.

questions.stem: Pencil pine (Athrotaxis cupressoides) stands on the Central Plateau were burnt in 2016. Surveys found that very few severely burnt stems resprouted. Why does this make the species vulnerable to fire?
options: Its seedlings grow fastest on ash beds, so fire leads to dense regrowth that self-thins
It lacks a reliable way to recover after severe fire, so burnt stands may not regenerate
Its seeds need fire to germinate, so unburnt stands cannot produce any new seedlings
Its thick bark protects every stem, so fire only ever kills the young trees growing at the forest edge
questions.explanation: Studies after the 2016 fires found that severely burnt pencil pine stems did not resprout and seedling regeneration was poor. With no reliable recovery mechanism, fire can permanently remove stands of this slow-growing conifer.

questions.stem: A land manager considers burning a block every 5 years. Which pairing correctly predicts the effect of this regime on two different Tasmanian communities?
options: Wet sclerophyll forest would turn into rainforest, while dry sclerophyll forest would become open alpine heath
Dry sclerophyll forest would persist with a simpler understorey, while rainforest at the edge would be lost
Rainforest would expand into the block, while dry sclerophyll forest would turn into mixed forest
Alpine heath would thrive on the extra nutrients, while buttongrass moorland would turn into rainforest
questions.explanation: Dry sclerophyll eucalypts resprout after low-intensity fire, so the forest persists, although very frequent fire can remove fire-sensitive shrubs. Rainforest species are fire-sensitive, so frequent burning kills them at the edge. Frequent fire pushes vegetation away from rainforest, not towards it.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly links fire frequency to Tasmanian vegetation?
options: Very frequent fire favours buttongrass, moderate fire favours eucalypt forest, and rare fire favours rainforest
Very frequent fire favours rainforest, moderate fire favours buttongrass, and rare fire favours eucalypt forest
Very frequent fire favours alpine heath, moderate fire favours rainforest, and rare fire favours grassland
Fire frequency has no effect, because rainfall alone decides where each vegetation type is found
questions.explanation: In western Tasmania, fire frequency strongly shapes vegetation: frequent fire maintains buttongrass moorland, intermediate intervals allow eucalypt forests, and long fire-free periods allow rainforest. Rainfall matters too, but fire modifies what each site supports.

questions.stem: Three western Tasmanian sites receive similar rainfall. Site A last burnt 8 years ago, site B 70 years ago and site C more than 400 years ago. Which vegetation sequence from A to C best fits these fire histories?
options: Rainforest, then eucalypt forest, then buttongrass moorland
Eucalypt forest, then rainforest, then buttongrass moorland
Rainforest, then buttongrass moorland, then eucalypt forest
Buttongrass moorland, then eucalypt forest, then rainforest
questions.explanation: Recently and frequently burnt sites in the wet west carry buttongrass, intermediate fire intervals allow eucalypt forest, and sites unburnt for centuries can develop rainforest. Rainforest is the vegetation least able to cope with recent fire, so it fits site C, not site A.

questions.stem: Many rivers in western Tasmania are dark brown like tea. What causes this colour?
options: Iron oxide dust blown from the dry Midlands during summer storms
Dense blooms of brown algae fed by fertiliser runoff from farms
Tannins and other organic compounds leached from peaty soils and plants
Fine clay particles eroded from cleared farmland in the catchment
questions.explanation: Water draining buttongrass moorland and peaty soils carries dissolved tannins and humic substances that stain it brown. It is usually clear rather than muddy, so suspended clay is not the cause.

questions.stem: At Ninepin Point and in Port Davey, tannin-stained fresh water forms a layer over the sea. Divers find deep-water species living unusually close to the surface. Why?
options: The fresh surface layer is saltier than the seawater below, so deep-water species are drawn up towards it
The tannins add nutrients that deep-water species need, so they rise to feed on them
The fresh water is warmer than the sea below, so deep-water species rise to warm up
The dark surface layer absorbs light, so shallow water is as dim as much deeper water elsewhere
questions.explanation: Tannin-stained water sharply reduces light penetration, so a few metres down the conditions resemble those at much greater depth in clear water. Fresh water is less salty than seawater, not more, which is why it floats on top.

questions.stem: A highland lake on the Central Plateau is compared with a lowland river pool. Which difference is most likely, because of altitude?
options: The highland lake is warmer, so it holds less dissolved oxygen and has a longer growing season
The highland lake is saltier, because evaporation is greater at high altitude
The highland lake is more turbid, because high-altitude catchments are mostly farmland
The highland lake is colder, so it holds more dissolved oxygen and has a shorter growing season
questions.explanation: Higher altitude means lower air and water temperatures. Cold water holds more dissolved oxygen, but low temperatures, frost and ice shorten the growing season for aquatic plants and animals.

questions.stem: Which is a disturbance that can reset a freshwater stream ecosystem in Tasmania?
options: A steady daily rise and fall of water temperature through a mild summer
Seasonal leaf fall from streamside trees that feeds invertebrate shredders
Regular overnight fall in dissolved oxygen as aquatic plants stop photosynthesis
A major flood that scours the streambed and removes plants and invertebrates
questions.explanation: A disturbance is a relatively sudden event that removes organisms and changes conditions, such as a flood, fire in the catchment or a pollution spill. Daily temperature and oxygen changes and leaf fall are normal cycles the community is adapted to.

questions.stem: An estuary such as the Derwent or the Tamar is best defined as:
options: an offshore reef where cold, nutrient-rich water rises from the ocean floor
a coastal lagoon fed only by rain, with no connection to rivers or the sea
a partly enclosed body of water where river fresh water mixes with seawater
a freshwater lake formed where a glacier once carved a deep mountain basin
questions.explanation: An estuary is where fresh river water meets and mixes with tidal seawater, giving a salinity gradient from fresh to marine. A glacial lake has no seawater input.

questions.stem: Macquarie Harbour on the west coast is a salt-wedge estuary. Which description of its water column is correct?
options: Seawater cannot enter the harbour, so the whole water column is fresh water from the rivers
Less dense river water flows out at the surface over denser seawater that moves in along the bottom
Denser river water sinks to the bottom while the lighter seawater floats on the surface and flows out to sea
River water and seawater mix completely, so salinity is the same from surface to bottom
questions.explanation: Fresh water is less dense than seawater, so in a salt-wedge estuary river water flows seaward at the surface while a wedge of salty water moves in along the bottom. Mixing between the layers is limited, which is why the deeper water can become low in oxygen.

questions.stem: Bottom water in Macquarie Harbour is often low in dissolved oxygen. Which combination of factors best explains this?
options: Strong layering limits mixing of oxygen-rich surface water downward, and organic matter decomposing at depth uses oxygen
Fresh surface water contains no oxygen, and seawater entering along the bottom is always free of oxygen
High salinity at depth prevents oxygen from dissolving, and tides pump oxygen out through the harbour mouth
Bright sunlight at depth drives photosynthesis that uses oxygen, and low temperatures release oxygen from water
questions.explanation: The fresh surface layer floats on denser seawater, so oxygen from the air and from the surface does not easily reach deeper water. Decomposers breaking down organic matter at depth consume oxygen, and it is replaced mainly when new seawater flows in along the bottom.

questions.stem: In an estuary, salinity (in parts per thousand) is measured 10 km upstream of the mouth: 4 at the surface and 29 near the bottom. At the mouth it is 31 at the surface and 33 near the bottom. What do these data show?
options: River water sinks below seawater upstream, so the bottom there is the freshest layer
The water column is fully mixed upstream, so salinity is the same at every depth there
Seawater cannot reach the upstream site, so all of its water must come from the river
A wedge of seawater extends upstream along the bottom beneath a fresher surface layer
questions.explanation: Upstream, the surface is nearly fresh while the bottom is almost as salty as seawater, so dense seawater has pushed upstream along the bed under the outflowing river water. A 25-unit difference between surface and bottom rules out a fully mixed water column.

questions.stem: Why are estuaries usually among the most productive ecosystems along the Tasmanian coast?
options: They receive nutrients from river runoff and tidal exchange, and shallow water lets light reach plants
They have constant salinity and temperature, so organisms living there never need to tolerate any change
They are too deep for light to reach the bottom, so decomposers release nutrients in the dark
They are isolated from rivers and the sea, so nutrients are never lost from the system
questions.explanation: Rivers deliver nutrients and sediment, tides bring in marine nutrients and flush wastes, and shallow, well-lit water supports seagrass, algae and phytoplankton. Salinity and temperature in estuaries vary a great deal, which is a challenge rather than a cause of high productivity.

questions.stem: Organisms in the upper Tamar estuary near Launceston face salinity that changes with each tide and after heavy rain. Which organisms are best suited to live there?
options: Deep-ocean species that require constant temperature and salinity
Species with a wide salinity tolerance range that can regulate their water balance
Species with a narrow salinity tolerance range adapted to full-strength seawater
Strictly freshwater species that cannot survive in any salty water
questions.explanation: Estuarine salinity fluctuates with tides and river flow, so residents need a broad tolerance range for salinity and ways to control water and salt balance. Species with narrow tolerance would spend much of the time in their zone of stress.

questions.stem: Coastal upwelling increases the productivity of marine ecosystems because it:
options: carries warm, nutrient-poor tropical water down onto the continental shelf
washes fresh water and sediment from rivers out to the edge of the shelf
pushes surface plankton down to the seabed where light is unavailable
brings cold, nutrient-rich deep water up into the sunlit surface layer
questions.explanation: Winds can drive surface water offshore, and deep water rich in nitrate and phosphate rises to replace it. In the sunlit surface, these nutrients fuel phytoplankton growth that supports the food web.

questions.stem: Giant kelp forests off eastern Tasmania have declined by about 95%. Scientists link this to the East Australian Current reaching further south. How would this change affect kelp?
options: The current brings colder, nutrient-rich water, so kelp grows too fast and breaks off in storms
The current brings fresh water from rivers, so the lower salinity kills the kelp holdfasts
The current brings clearer water, so too much light reaches the seabed and bleaches the young kelp fronds
The current brings warmer, nutrient-poor water, so kelp lacks the cool, nutrient-rich water it needs
questions.explanation: Giant kelp grows best in cool water with high nutrient levels. The strengthening East Australian Current carries warm, nutrient-poor water south along the east coast, stressing kelp. Warmer water has also let the long-spined sea urchin spread south and graze reefs bare.

questions.stem: A study compares two Tasmanian reefs. Reef P is near a river mouth after heavy rain; reef Q is on an exposed headland. Reef P shows turbid water and fewer kelp plants at depth. Which explanation best fits?
options: Runoff makes the water clearer, so kelp at depth is exposed to too much light and dies back
Runoff removes all nutrients from the water, so the river mouth is the least productive part of the coast
Runoff carries sediment that reduces light at depth, and lower salinity near the river mouth stresses marine organisms
Runoff raises salinity near the river mouth, and the extra salt prevents kelp spores from settling
questions.explanation: Land runoff delivers sediment that clouds the water and reduces the light reaching kelp at depth, and fresh water lowers salinity. Runoff can add nutrients rather than remove them, and fresh water lowers salinity rather than raising it.

questions.stem: Which feature most distinguishes the rocky intertidal zone from the subtidal reef below it?
options: Organisms receive no sunlight, so the community depends entirely on food falling from above
Organisms live in fresh water, so they never experience salt or wave action at any time
Organisms are exposed to air at low tide, with large swings in temperature, salinity and moisture
Organisms are always submerged, so temperature and salinity stay constant throughout the day and night
questions.explanation: The intertidal zone is covered and uncovered by the tides, so its organisms face drying, heating, cooling and salinity changes when exposed. The subtidal zone stays underwater, so conditions are much more stable.
